shared_text:
The flight. A twin-engine airliner on a visual approach, in daylight and visual conditions, to an airport reached through a valley.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring. The captain had about 21,000 hours but had flown into this airport only once, on a check flight; the first officer had not been there many times, nor for several months. They had briefed the approach thoroughly.

What happened. On the first approach, flying manually at 1,100 ft, the captain crossed a ridgeline believed to be the correct one and banked hard left into a valley. It was the wrong one. When the wings levelled, the first officer recognised this and called for a go-around, which the captain flew. On the second approach the captain identified the runway, ridgeline and valley before the first waypoint. Again flying manually at 1,100 ft, the captain turned into the valley early, leaving the aircraft high on the profile, and descended to reach the landing zone. The first officer called descent rates of 1,100 and 1,200 ft per minute, which the captain acknowledged. At about 1,400 ft per minute the first officer called for a go-around, and the ground proximity warning sounded "Sink rate", then "Pull up". The captain said no: the runway was now in sight and the captain was already correcting towards stable approach criteria. The first officer saw the captain correcting and was ready to call again. The captain continued the approach and landed.
safe_outcome: On short final the descent rate was 900 ft per minute and the speed was correct, with no further alerts, and the aircraft touched down on speed within the first 1,000 ft of the runway. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: The aircraft could not be stopped on the remaining runway. It left the end of the runway at about 30 knots and came to rest on the grass. The passengers were evacuated, and two received minor injuries during the evacuation. The aircraft was slightly damaged.
notes: Rule 3 removed: both "Cause" and "Suggestions" sections (the captain's view that unfamiliarity and the long gap since the check flight caused both events, "unlike any other in my 35 years" and "extremely challenging", the proposal for repeated line checks, the first officer's "be more cautious" and "more situationally aware"), and narrative 2's heading "Correcting an unstable approach and not going around". Kept from the Cause sections as facts: the captain's 21,000 hours, the single earlier visit on a check flight, the first officer's few visits and none for several months, and the thorough briefing. Rule 5 moved to the safe ending: back to 900 ft per minute and the correct speed on short final with no further alerts, and the on-speed touchdown within the first 1,000 ft. Omitted for length: the reason for the downwind entry (early sight of the runway), crossing the shoreline at 1,200 ft fully configured at 129 knots, the cloud at about 2,000 ft, the 2 seconds in the wrong valley, the hold and the FMS reload with the first officer flying, and the captain's review of flight data, video and notes before the flight. Judgement call: the narratives differ on whether the GPWS warning came before or after the first officer's go-around call (narrative 1 puts it before, narrative 2 roughly at the same time), so the text joins them with "and" without ordering them.
